implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: a header-only Jinja-style engine such as inja holds the layout and fragments as templates, {% include "partials/row.html" %} is the placeholder, {{ ... }} binds the model, and inja::Environment::render/write is the View Manager - templates stay editable as data instead of being compiled into the page function. inja needs C++17 (std::string_view, std::variant, std::filesystem); keep Template objects cached in request paths so parsing happens once, and fall back to hand-written fragment functions for tiny, dependency-free pages.
pitfalls: inja re-parses on every render unless the parsed inja::Template is kept alive; parse once per process and render many times.
Include paths are resolved against the environment root at render time - a path assembled from request data is a template-injection/local-file-disclosure risk.
Missing template variables throw by default (or silently render empty if a default callback is installed), so the data contract of embedded fragments must be documented per template.

variants.name: Hand-written fragment functions returning std::string
variants.idiom_name: std::string fragment functions composed by the page function
variants.implementation_notes: Before any engine, C++ composed pages from ordinary functions: each fragment returns std::string (or appends to a std::ostringstream/std::string), the page function concatenates the pieces in layout order, parameters are function arguments and escaping is a central helper. This remains the right choice for small, dependency-free or freestanding pages, where an engine's parsing and data model would cost more than the markup it manages; the price is that every markup change is a recompile.
pitfalls: Composing by repeated concatenation reallocates per fragment; append into one reused std::string/std::ostringstream and reserve when the size is known.
Hand-written escaping: without a single escape helper (or a library such as html.hpp) any fragment that interpolates user data emits it raw.
